en: Now, therefore, we shall explain the method of meditative absorption for the Paramahaṃsas.

That which is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being) is Brahman variegated by ignorance (avidyā). From Brahman comes the Unmanifest (avyakta); from the Unmanifest, the Great Principle (mahat); from the Great Principle, the Ego (ahaṃkāra); from the Ego, the five subtle elements (tanmātras); from the five subtle elements, the five gross elements (mahābhūtas); and from the five gross elements, the entire universe.

Having divided each of the five elements into two parts, and having set aside one half for itself, the other half is divided into four parts which are then joined to the others; this is the quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), by which the form of Māyā—which is essentially free from phenomenal proliferation—is made to appear as such through the methods of superimposition (adhyāropa) and negation (apavāda).

Oṃ. The five gross elements, having been made fivefold (pañcīkṛta), and all their effects, are called Virāṭ. This is the gross body of the Self. The perception of objects through the senses is the waking state. The Self who identifies with both of these is Viśva. These three constitute the letter A.

The five unquintuplicated great elements are the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*); their effects are the seventeenfold subtle body (*liṅga*), consisting of the five vital breaths, the ten organs, the mind, and the intellect. This elemental subtle body is called *Hiraṇyagarbha*. It is the subtle body of the Self. When the instruments [of perception] have been withdrawn, a cognition arising from the impressions of the waking state, accompanied by its objects, is called dream. The Self that identifies with both of these is the *Taijasa*. These three constitute the letter *U*.

The ignorance of the Self (*ātmājñāna*), which is the cause of the two bodies and is accompanied by appearance (*sābhāsa*), is called the "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*). This is the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*) of the Self. And that is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; it is neither different, nor non-different, nor both different and non-different from anything whatsoever; it is neither partless, nor possessed of parts, nor both. Rather, it is to be removed solely by the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman. Deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is the state of the intellect (*buddhi*) abiding as the causal self when all forms of cognition have been withdrawn. The Self who identifies with both of these is the "wise one" (*prājña*). These three constitute the letter *M*.
The letter *a* is in *u*; *u* is in *m*; and *m* is in the syllable *oṃ*, which is none other than the Self (*aham*).

I am the Self, the witness, pure and consisting solely of the nature of consciousness; I am neither ignorance nor its effect. Rather, I am indeed Brahman—the innermost consciousness—abiding non-differently as "I am Brahman," which is by nature eternally pure, enlightened, liberated, and true, and which is non-dual supreme bliss. This is supported by such scriptural texts as: "That thou art," "Brahman am I," "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," and "This Self is Brahman. Thus concludes the *Pañcīkaraṇa*.
Thus, in the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya).
